title: Drug-coated balloon dilatation catheter for transurethral treatment of urethral strictures
summary:
Urethral strictures are a significant urological condition that primarily affects men and can lead to significant impairments in quality of life. Patients often suffer from a weak, thin, or twisted urine stream, as well as dribbling at the end of the urinary tract. These symptoms not only impair physical function but also have far-reaching effects on the psychological well-being and social participation of those affected.
Various treatment options are available, ranging from minimally invasive procedures to complex reconstructive surgeries. Among them is internal urethrotomy (UI), also known as urethral slitting, which is currently the standard treatment for urethral strictures.
However, at least 50-60% of treated patients experience a recurrence, i.e., the stricture recurs, after 3-9 months. The structural freedom rate is in the single-digit percentage range.
In recent years, innovative treatment approaches, particularly the use of drug-coated balloon dilatation catheters (DCBs), have gained traction. This technology combines mechanical dilation, i.e., the widening of the stricture, with the local administration of medications designed to influence the scar tissue and prevent re-healing. A commonly used drug for this coating is paclitaxel, which inhibits cell division and thus is intended to reduce excessive scarring.
The study aims to investigate whether treatment with a balloon catheter is superior to the current standard treatment, UI, and whether it represents a better long-term treatment option for patients.
Patients who meet the inclusion criteria and decide to participate in the study will be randomly assigned to one of two treatment groups. One group (Arm 1) will receive treatment with the balloon catheter, and the other (Arm 2) will receive the standard treatment (internal urethrotomy - UI). The assignment is made randomly, similar to a lottery.
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Capacity to consent  
- Existence of a consent form dated and signed by the patient  
- Compliance of the patient 
- Willingness to participate in the one-year follow-up phase  
- Cystoscopic or urethrogram-confirmed diagnosis of symptomatic, short-segment recurrent stricture of the anterior urethra (≤ 2 cm)  
- At least 1 previous UI due to short-segment urethral stricture of the anterior urethra (≤ 2 cm)
Exclusion criteria:
- Previous or current participation in studies with the same indication
- Previous Optilume® surgery
- Known hypersensitivity and/or severe allergies to paclitaxel or structural analogues or other components of the medical device
- Patients with strictures that cannot be passed with a 0.038-inch (0.97 mm) guidewire
- History of anterior urethral urethroplasty 
- Previous hypospadias repair
- Diagnosis of lichen sclerosus or stricture due to balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO)
- Transurethral resection of a bladder tumor (TURB) within 6 weeks prior to study enrollment
- Presence of an artificial urethral sphincter, loops or stents in the urethra or prostate 
- Existing bladder or urinary tract infection 
- Obstructive voiding symptom not attributable to the stricture 
- Benign bladder neck stricture 
- Radical prostatectomy 
- Untreated stress incontinence 
- Radiation cystitis 
- Overactive bladder 
- Known neurogenic bladder, sphincter abnormalities or poor detrusor muscle function 
- Untreated or progressive prostate cancer 
- Bladder tumors that, due to their location and/or size, obstruct urine flow or significantly complicate catheterization
- Chronic renal failure and treatment with haemodialysis 
- Currently uncontrolled diabetes (haemoglobin A1c > 8.0%) or signs of poor wound healing due to diabetes
- Suspected or diagnosed primary neurological disease, such as multiple sclerosis or Parkinson's disease, or other neurological disease impairing bladder, sphincter or detrusor muscle function
- Current use of alpha-blockers, anticonvulsants and antispasmodics, or use within the last 4 weeks prior to study inclusion
- Regular use or planned use of botulinum toxin A (onabotulinumtoxinA) in the urinary tract within the next 90 days
- Clinically relevant invisible or visible hematuria, or hematuria with suspected bladder cancer or other urothelial tumors
- Ongoing or completed within the last 6 months systemic chemotherapy or immunosuppressive therapy, as well as ongoing or completed within the last 6 months radiotherapy in the lesser pelvic region
- Unwillingness to have protected sexual intercourse for 30 days after treatment
- Unwillingness to have protected sexual intercourse or to abstain for 90 days after treatment if the sexual partner is fertile 
- Existing PSA levels that are considered suspicious for prostate cancer according to current guidelines and clinical assessment
